en: Oṃ, homage to Śrī Heruka!

Having prostrated with my head to that Śrī Heruka by whom the entire web of conceptual constructions has been uprooted through the meditation on the sequence of mudrās, I likewise proclaim this to the gurus here.
Therefore, having properly received a small portion of this instruction through the exhortation of a virtuous disciple,
I shall now fully elucidate it with clear words for their benefit, as it has been proclaimed [and previously explained].

For here, first of all, a yogin who has faith in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Tantra* must become one whose ordinary ego-grasping has been eliminated; therefore, for that purpose, the Blessed One first set forth the initial instruction on the purification of the aggregates and sense-bases.

Then, since the cultivation of the state of a Tathāgata—that is, the cultivation of the mundane and supramundane paths—must be performed, there is the instruction on the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) for the purpose of demonstrating that. Furthermore, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are the second instruction, consisting of the deities of the thirty-sevenfold maṇḍala circle for the person who has faith in the Mantra Mahāyāna. For the purpose of demonstrating that, the third is the instruction on the purification of the deities of the factors conducive to awakening.

Since the establishment of the deities of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) is comprised within five wheels, two wheels are established for the deities [of the first two wheels] by virtue of their being under the sovereignty of the Lord of the Maṇḍala. The fourth is the "Instruction on Heroes" (*vīranirdeśa*), intended to explain the means (*upāya*) in the form of lords for the Heroines (*vīraṇī*) established in the remaining three wheels.

And since one must know in which location those aforementioned deities, whose nature consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), are to be meditated upon, the fifth is the "Instruction on Locations" (*sthānanirdeśa*).
The sixth [chapter], the "Instruction on the Signs such as Facial Color," is for the purpose of describing the facial colors, marks, and so forth of these very deities just mentioned.

The seventh, the "Instruction on the Two Armors," is for the purpose of stating the two types of armor for the sake of protecting the mandala circle, which has been perfected in the form of wisdom and means. The eighth, the "Instruction on the Summoning of the Wisdom Circle," is for the purpose of demonstrating that the meditation on the two armors must be preceded by the entry of the wisdom circle.

Starting from the first exposition just mentioned, the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has been summarized; thus, the ninth exposition concerns the manifestation of its nature as the three bodies (*kāyatraya*). Once the mandala circle has been cultivated, the tenth exposition concerns the offering of the *bali* and the observance of the tenth day (*daśamī*), performed respectively for the sake of pacifying all obstacles and for the purpose of internal worship (*adhyātmikapūjā*).
Since complete purification does not occur through such cultivation alone, the eleventh exposition concerns universal purification (*sarvaviśuddhi*).

Following that, the twelfth [chapter] is the instruction on the single word that determines the reality of all mantras, which is to be explained by means of the aforementioned meditation on the conventional and ultimate truths as far as possible.

Following that, the thirteenth is the instruction on the non-duality resulting from the determination of all vehicles through the *āli* and *kāli*, preceded by the explanation of the summary of external locations such as the *pīṭhas* and so forth, and the ritual for determining all mantras as stated in the twelfth chapter.

Immediately following that, the fourteenth [chapter] is the instruction on the hand-worship (*hastapūjā*) associated with the union of the four heroes (*caturvīrasaṃyoga*), in order to explain the specific signs (*saṃketa*) consisting primarily of hand-gestures (*karacchomā*) by means of a distinguished ego-sense (*viśiṣṭāhaṃkāra*).

The fifteenth [chapter] is the instruction on the conduct-vow (*caryāvrata*), for the purpose of performing the conduct-vow and so forth by a yogin who abides in the aforementioned distinguished hand-gestures and the like.

Even if a yogi remains established in such practices, vows, and so forth, if he does not attain accomplishment (*siddhi*) very quickly, then, in order to generate confidence regarding the specific types of accomplishment, there is the sixteenth chapter, the *Instruction on the Determination of Accomplishment* (*Siddhiniścaya-śrīherukīkaraṇanirdeśa*). Once confidence has arisen regarding the specific types of accomplishment, one must investigate the purpose and so forth of the purification of the Lord of the Mandala, the deities of the retinue, and others; for that purpose, there is the seventeenth chapter, the *Instruction on the Purification of Reality* (*Tattvaviśuddhinirdeśa*), which explains those matters.
This is the sequence of the chapters on meditation (*bhāvanā*).
Now, for the purpose of introducing the tantra, he first states the promise to explain it, beginning with "atha ata" and so forth.
Herein there are three topics:
the promise to explain, the purpose, and the summary meaning along with the meaning of the words.

Therein, the first part is fivefold: (1) generating the conviction regarding the excellence of the teacher’s authority in his teaching; (2) causing the audience to pay close attention; (3) bringing together a group of disciples who were not previously assembled; (4) establishing the skill of the commentator regarding the methods of exposition; and (5) indicating that this [teaching] follows upon the *Vṛhat-tantra*.

Regarding the presentation of the five topics, beginning with the summary of the essential meaning (*piṇḍārtha*), it should be understood that this tantra is called the *Yoginī-saṃcāra* because it teaches the procedure for the movement (*saṃcāra*) of the Yoginīs, as stated in the passage: "I shall fully explain the procedure for the movement."

By this [verse], the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is primarily presented as a constituent part [of the path], while the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is not [presented here] by way of its absence.

The two stages are the subject matter; and by means of demonstrating the removal of the doubt regarding their pointlessness through the line, "By which mere consciousness the practitioner may attain accomplishment" (1.3), the purpose is established.
Furthermore, within the conjunction of the thirty-seven principles (*tattva*), the remaining portion of the generation stage as a constituent part of the subject matter—eternality—is stated.

The relationship between the expression and the expressed, characterized as that of the communicator and the communicated, is implied by the sense. Furthermore, the purpose is the production of such accomplishment for others after one has attained personal accomplishment regarding the expressed object through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. As for the meaning of the words, the connection is: "Now I shall fully explain the procedure for the transition [to the next stage]."

In this context, the word *atha* (now/then) has the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*), as in the phrase "Now follows the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*). Alternatively, it has the sense of "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*), as in "Now Vajradhara... Alternatively, it signifies "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), because this [work] follows immediately after the teaching of the Root Tantra, due to its being the medium-sized mandala within the Great Tantra, or because it is taught immediately after the teaching of the Root Tantra. As it has been said: "It refers back to what was previously introduced," and so forth.

By the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he highlights that the members of the assembly are endowed with distinguished qualities such as faith. Since I have been requested by a multitude of heroic men and women possessed of qualities like faith, preceded by the performance of distinguished offerings and so forth, the meaning is: "Therefore, for the sake of future fortunate beings to understand the subtle Root Tantra, I shall fully proclaim the ritual procedure for the movement [of the deities].

Regarding "I shall fully proclaim" (*saṃpravakṣyāmi*): it means I shall correctly, without error, and extensively explain by way of detailed analysis, because [the procedure] was mostly unclear in the Root Tantra. I shall speak; I shall declare—this is the meaning.

"Regarding the procedure for movement (*saṃcāravidhi*): it is the method for the practice of benefiting sentient beings by generating and relying upon a body of a specific form, which consists of the movement of the *yoginīs* situated within the maṇḍala-circle throughout the three or five wheels (*cakras*). Its procedure is the means of generation according to circumstances through one of the stages such as the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*).
Of what nature is it? It is "supreme" (*uttama*), because it is superior due to being the antidote to ordinary ego-clinging (*ahaṃkāra*)."

If I were to explain the procedure for transference (*saṃcāra*), what would be the purpose of explaining it? Or rather, what is this procedure for transference? To this he says: "It is to be cultivated" (*bhāvanīyam*). Once the procedure for transference has been taught, those two [aspects] that have been heard and reflected upon must be practiced repeatedly until they reach the state of becoming one's very nature (*sātmabhāva*). "Consisting of the three wheels" (*tricakrātmā*) means consisting of the three wheels through the divisions of mind, speech, and body. By this, the essential nature of the procedure for transference is stated.

By whom is it to be cultivated? He says: "Established on the path of yoga. Regarding the explanation [of the phrase] "by persons established therein": here, *yoga* refers to a specific meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consisting of the cultivation of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) through the application of instantaneous forms and so forth; its *mārga* (path) consists of the seed-mantras (*mantrabīja*) which serve as the means (*upāya*). "Established therein" means by those who are intent upon it, being firmly established through specific modes of cultivation. || 1 ||

One might object: "Is not the teaching on the procedure for the movement [of the vital winds] unnecessary, since the Blessed One himself has already taught it in both the extensive and subtle forms of the *Mūlatantra*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It was concealed" (*gopitam*). Although spoken by the Blessed One, it was kept hidden from those unworthy beings who pride themselves on being their own readers of the scriptures. "That which" refers to the subject matter characterized by the procedure for movement. "In that manner" means in a perfectly clear way. "Where? he asks; he replies: "In the *Tantra*. This refers to the work titled the *Lakṣābhidhāna* and its extracted portions. In this context, *tantra* refers to a continuous composition.
And that [tantra] is threefold, distinguished by way of cause, fruit, and means.
Among these, the *dharmadhātu*—which is without beginning or end—is the tantra of the cause (*hetutantra*).
The cultivation of the two stages as they occur, which serves as the means for the direct realization of the *dharmadhātu*, is the tantra of the means (*upāyatantra*).

The *phalatantra* (result-tantra) is the realization of the state of Śrī Heruka, which consists in the direct perception of the pure dharmadhātu and is attainable through the power of the causal tantra (*hetutantra*) and the long-term cultivation of the method-tantra (*upāyatantra*).
Furthermore, the collection of words that explains this is also called "tantra" by way of metaphorical designation.

Regarding the phrase "in that [state], it is situated in reverse order" (*anulomavisaṃsthita*): it means it is situated even by way of sequence (*anukrama*) and arrangement (*paripāṭī*), yet it is situated through separation (*vihāya*), meaning it is not established in a regular sequence at all. Consequently, because the procedure for the transition (*saṃcāra-vidhi*) is not established in a regular sequence, it is proven that the teaching in the *Saṃcāra-tantra* is indeed purposeful.

In some manuscripts, the reading "anulomavilomataḥ" (by direct and reverse order) is seen. According to that view, the teacher must explain how it is concealed. It is concealed by means of both sequential and non-sequential order, as it has been said: "In the Tantra, the left [side] first expands to the right, and likewise the subtle. Consequently, this means it is concealed by the sequence of counter-clockwise and clockwise rotation.

Furthermore, he asks "How so? and says: "The enumeration" (*uddeśam*). This refers to that which resembles the mere description of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) as it has not yet been unfolded through an unerring explanation. "In what manner" (*yathā*) means by whatever method. "Proclaimed" (*proktam*) means as stated in the *Bṛhatī* Tantra itself. "The exposition" (*nirdeśam*) is a comparison based on the reversal of the previous [state]. "In that very way" (*tathaiva*) means by virtue of its being concealed. || 2 ||
"Pratinirdeśam" (Detailed Exposition) means the presentation of the subject matter free from doubt through the fulfillment of all its constituent parts.

Alternatively, "Uddeśa" (Summary) refers to the Body of Instruction (*nirdeśakāya*), because it is taught by way of indicating the individuals who are inclined toward it. "Nirdeśa" (Exposition) refers to the Form of the Enjoyment Body (*sāṃbhogikakāya*), because it provides the detailed exposition of the sublime Dharma for the assembly of Bodhisattvas who are masters of the ten stages. "Pratinirdeśa" (Detailed Exposition) refers to that which is taught specifically for those [Bodhisattvas] alone, as it is the exclusive domain of the Buddhas.
"Entirely" (*samasta*) means that it is exhaustive in its particulars, by describing the subject matter and incidental topics and by clearing away the doubts of the assembly as the occasion arises.

Alternatively, "entirely" means that it is complete in its entirety by describing the characteristics of the *yoginīs* and so forth. "The rule of convention" (*saṃketavidhi*) refers to the presentation of specific modes of communication and the like, through the exposition of physical and verbal gestures (*kāyavākchomā*).

"What kind? "Supreme. It is superior by virtue of its distinction from the conventional discourse of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). If the procedure for the movement [of the winds] is taught in the previously explained explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*) by the Blessed One through both direct and reverse order, as well as through summary, detailed exposition, and further explanation, and if it is heard, reflected upon, and cultivated by listeners established on the path of yoga, then what would be the fruit of that cultivation for them? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By which... (yeneti).

By means of the procedure for circulation (*saṃcāravidhi*), which was concealed in the Root Tantra but taught here; and by the listeners having cultivated it through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditation; "merely by knowing" means merely by practicing through the sequence of hearing and so forth. "The practitioner" (*sādhaka*) refers to the yogi who, relying on the means of mantra, mudrā, and so on, accomplishes the state of Śrī Heruka, whose nature consists of the three bodies. "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, characterized as both mundane and supramundane. "He shall obtain" (*āpnuyāt*) means he shall attain it. "I shall explain such a procedure for circulation"—this is the connection with what precedes. (3)
Regarding what was stated as "the self of the three wheels," he states its remainder: "by thirty-seven" means by the number thirty-seven;
"by yoga" means by the practice, or by the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) characterized by any one [of the deities] beginning with Jhaṭiti.

"Factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣāḥ*): enlightenment (*bodhi*) is that which has attained purity immediately following the cultivation of the diamond-like meditative absorption (*vajropamasamādhi*), the culmination of the cultivation of the five paths; the "factors" (*pakṣāḥ*) are those which exist within that [enlightenment] because they are conducive to it. These are they.

"Established" means that here, in this system of mantra (*mantranaya*), according to the principle stated in the third chapter which is to be explained, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth are themselves established in the form of deities within the five wheels (*cakras*).
What are those factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*)? He says: "In the world," meaning starting from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

"Having manifested" means having first understood them through the sequence of hearing and so forth in their essential nature consisting of wisdom, vigor, concentration, and so on; having reflected upon them as they truly are; and having cultivated them through meditation until they reach the limit of firm establishment through excellence.
"Renowned" means well-known in the *Pāramitādarśana*.

If this is so, and their cultivation is appropriate exactly as they are established in the *Pāramitā* system, then one might ask: why should there be a further cultivation of them here in the Mantra system? To this he says: "The supreme world of Śrī Heruka. This refers to the world of Śrī Heruka—who possesses four faces and twelve arms and whose nature is the four liberations—as being supreme and excellent, consisting of the thirty-seven forms such as the Ḍākinīs and others, which are comprised within the side of purification (*vyavadāna*).

Having established that they move by depending on the totality of causes and conditions characterized by the transformation of mantras, symbols, and so forth, the meaning is that those very factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) consist of the thirty-seven deities of the maṇḍala. || 4 ||

The external commentary (*bāhyavyākhyā*): "Now, therefore," and so forth, as before. Regarding the phrase "the method of movement" (*saṃcāravidhim*): the "movement" (*saṃcāra*) is the wandering or going (*caraṇa-gamana*) of the channels (*nāḍī*) characterized by being indivisible and so forth, which exist externally as the constituents (*dhātu*) such as nails and teeth; the "method" (*vidhi*) is the sequence of experiencing that [movement], preceded by the indication of internal breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). The connection with what precedes is: "I shall fully explain that. Of what nature is it? "Supreme" (*uttama*); it is excellent because, by avoiding the external proliferation (*prapañca*), it is characterized by the activity arising from the very concealed bodhicitta.
"It should be meditated upon" means that the conventional *bodhicitta* itself should be experienced as non-different from the support and the supported.

Regarding "having the nature of the three wheels": just as in the external wheels of mind, speech, and body, the forms of the heroes and heroines such as Pracaṇḍa, Aṭaṅka, Kapāla, and so forth are meditated upon, in exactly the same way, within the internal locations such as the head and others, by means of the conventional *bodhicitta*—which is of the nature of passion—a person should rely on the union of wisdom and method and meditate upon it as having the very nature of the internal three wheels, in the form of the constituents such as nails and teeth, as non-different from that [external visualization].

He says this very thing: "on the path of yoga" (*yogamārge*). Yoga is the practice characterized by the three [stages] of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*); its path is that which extends from Śiraḥ, Pullīra, and Malaya (or their synonyms) up to Kulūtā. "Established therein" means it should be contemplated by those who dwell there and experience it.

"What is this path of yoga? he asks. It is "concealed," meaning covered over, because for the most part it has not been stated by his own mouth [the Blessed One]. "That which" refers to the nature of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth. "In that manner" means by way of a form consisting of unwavering certainty. "In the *tantra*" means in the root *tantra*, which exists in both extensive and subtle forms; for that [root *tantra*] is beyond the reach of ordinary beings and is accessible only through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Bodhisattvas. For this very reason, the sequence of the sections on dissolution and enjoyment (*bhoga*) has been demonstrated primarily by Vajrapāṇi, Vajragarbha, and others, since the Blessed One did not state it by his own mouth in the subtle root *tantra*.

To the question "How so?", he says: "In direct order" (*anuloma*). Starting from Pullīramalaya and ending at Kulūta, the sequence of experiencing those [sites] is the direct order (*anuloma*), whether by the power of breath-retention (*vāyudhāraṇā*) or by the application of the instruments (*karaṇa*).

And by the placement of the seed-syllables beginning with *Vyā*, according to possibility and with reference to individuals of weak, middling, or superior capacity, starting from Kulūta and ending at Pullīramalaya is the reverse order (*viloma*).
Therefore, he says "the instruction" (*uddeśa*) regarding the meaning of those two through the cultivation of such a sequence.
It refers to the sign of the external union of wisdom and means, or the instruction itself, as far as it has been taught.
As stated by the venerable Kṛṣṇapāda in the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*: "From the instruction [arise] the churner and the churning," and so forth.

"Yathā" means in whatever manner the liberation from conceptual construction occurs for individuals belonging to the class of those characterized by passion; "proktam" (spoken) means it was taught by the Blessed One as a means for experiencing reality (*tattva*); "nirdeśam" (the detailed instruction) is so called because it is the specific explanation of the limb of the *upasādhana*;
"tathaiva ca" (and in that very same way) means it was taught in that very same manner—as it was said: "The seat is separate from the detailed instruction."

"Exposition" (*pratinirdeśa*) is so called because the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) have been specified. "In its entirety" (*samasta*) is so called because the great member of the proof has the nature of the cessation of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
"The rule of convention" (*saṃketavidhi*) is so called because wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) are designated by this term "thus" (*evam*).
"Supreme" (*uttama*) means that even through the demonstration of the practice of passion (*rāgacaryā*), it is superior because it is solely devoted to reality (*tattva*).

"By this" (*yena*) refers to this very method of convention (*saṃketavidhi*). "Merely by knowing" (*vijñātamātreṇa*) means merely by experiencing. "The practitioner" (*sādhaka*) is one who cultivates the internal sequence (*āntarakrama*). "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the state [of the yogin] due to the firmness of his mind; the term is used here figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*). "He shall obtain" (*āpnuyāt*) means he shall attain. Regarding this very point, he states the preliminary action: "thirty-seven."
By this placement of the seed-syllables and mantra-letters in the left and right channels (*nāḍī*), the *mantraulī* is indicated. Through such yoga and application,
the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*) refers to that which has the characteristic of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) as its intended meaning.
In that [state], the causes established in the two wings are positioned.
By means of the knowledge of the yogin, conceptual constructions are set aside— the yogin, having perceived through the nature of the channels that which consists of the four wheels,
becomes manifest in the world by way of the form of the vital wind (*vāyu*).
“Renowned” means they are well-known in the Mantra Mahāyāna.

“Śrī Heruka” refers to that which pertains to the Blessed One, whose characteristic is the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*). “The world” (*jagat*) refers to that which is comprised within the realm of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*). “Supreme” (*parama*) means that the very form of the fire of gnosis takes on the aspect of Śrī Heruka; such is the meaning. (1–4)

Internal commentary: The phrase "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*) and so forth is as explained previously. Regarding "the procedure for the movement" (*saṃcāravidhim*): "movement" (*saṃcāraḥ*) refers to the practice of touching, embracing, and so forth, preceded by the experience of the innate (*sahaja*) through the analogy of the feet; it is the indication of the innate in the case of the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) according to the instruction. "Its procedure" (*asya vidhiḥ*) means the manner of experiencing; that [is what is meant].

"Supreme" (*uttama*) means that it is preeminent by virtue of having the nature of Mahāmudrā. "To be cultivated as the essence of the three wheels" (*bhāvanīyaṃ tricakrātma*) means that within the three wheels—beginning from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) through the three wheels such as the enjoyment wheel (*sambhogacakra*)—there is the descent of the *bodhicitta* from the head, the pervasion of all eight types of bliss, and the attainment of the vajra-base. Because this consists of the state of retaining the drop (*bindu*) in its jewel (*maṇi*), it has that as its essence.

Regarding "on the path of yoga" (*yogamārge*): yoga is the innate (*sahaja*) alone; on that [yoga], the "path" (*mārga*) is the way, which consists of the abandonment of conceptual constructions such as passion, within the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyayoga*).
"In that, they are established" means "there, they are grasped by the yogis.

Thus, this arisen fourth reality (*tattva*) was taught by the Blessed One in the *Tantra* in both gross and subtle forms; yet it was concealed in such a clear and formidable manner that it was not revealed at all to those who are unworthy vessels—as stated in the *Guhyasamāja Tantra*: "That fourth [reality] is likewise again" (18.112). This is because it is taught merely to such an extent.

"In direct and reverse order" means from the top of the head down to the tip of the *vajramaṇi*, and back up to the end of the head, because the element of consciousness (*cittadhātu*) takes the form of *dhāraṇā* through the power of the *dhāraṇās* of wind and the other elements.

"Uddeśa" refers to the experience of the state of Ānanda, because of the subtlety of the bliss. "Nirdeśa" refers to the supreme experience (paramānubhava), because it is an experience of bliss that is somewhat beyond the experience of [ordinary] pleasure, being distinct from equanimity (*upekṣā*).

"Pratinirdeśa" refers to the experience of *virama*, because, consisting of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*), it is even more intense than the former. "Samasta" refers to its perfection by way of being the nature of the experience of the two types of the innate (*sahaja*). "The rule of convention" (*saṃketavidhi*) refers to the necessity of relying upon the specific instructions of the Guru at the time of experiencing the two types of the innate, which take the form of instructions on states such as the illusion-like (*māyopama*).

"Supreme" (*uttama*) means that, by abandoning the [mere] co-emergent (*sahaja*) through the use of an illustration, it is superior because it is the cause for firmly grasping the very thing illustrated, according to the principle of conceptualization occurring subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"By which" refers to the aforementioned sequence of co-emergent experience.

"Merely by knowing" means by what is personally experienced and cultivated through the instruction of the guru. "The practitioner" (*sādhaka*) means one who accomplishes that [state] through the practice of the secret *maṇḍala* (*guhyauli*).
"Siddhim" means the attainment of the characteristic of reaching nirvāṇa in this very life; the meaning is that one shall obtain it. This refers to the accomplishment (siddhi) just mentioned.

Since all Buddhas become adorned with qualities, he says "thirty-seven" in order to demonstrate that, [meaning] by way of the characteristics of the applications of mindfulness and so forth. "By yoga" means by the practice comprised within the state of fruition.
"Bodhipakṣā" means that awakening (*bodhi*) is characterized by the ultimate, innate experience; "factors" (*pakṣā*) are so called because they serve as the means (*upāya*) toward it.
"Established" (*vyavasthitā*) means that within that very innate accomplishment (*sahajasiddhi*), there is no innate accomplishment apart from its qualities.

"In the world" (*loka*) refers to that which is comprised within the three realms. "Having cultivated" (*prabhāvya*) means having meditated upon the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) as being inseparable from the innate. "Renowned" (*vikhyātā*) means appearing within the mental continuum of yogis.

This is what is meant: just as the yogi himself experiences the fruit—which is inseparable from all the qualities of a Buddha—at the culmination of the direct realization of the fourth reality (*tattva*), so too does the entire triple world appear to him in that very same way, and not by way of its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

This is precisely what is stated in the phrase "the supreme world of Śrī Heruka. The meaning is that for him, the world becomes supreme—that is, excellent—only in its innate form (*sahajākāra*), and not in a form external to it;
in other words, he knows everything as having the form of Śrī Heruka. (1–4)

The Secret Explanation (*Guhyavyākhyā*): "Now, therefore," and so forth, as before. "I shall fully explain the procedure for the movement" (*saṃcāravidhi*) means: the movement (*saṃcāra*) of the deities throughout all the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*) according to their respective possibilities; the "procedure" (*vidhi*) refers to the method of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakāra*) for those beings who are to be trained (*vineya*) in their appropriate places. I shall describe that. By this, the summary of the first chapter is stated.

"Supreme" means that it is excellent because of the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and because of their merging with the assembly of deities residing in the five wheels; this is due to the demonstration of the unity of the modes of cultivation in the systems of the Perfections (*pāramitā*) and Mantra. By this, the summary of the second and third chapters is indicated.

"It should be cultivated as the essence of the three wheels" means that it consists of the three wheels through the division of the wheels of mind, speech, and body, because of their distribution (*vyāsa*) within the twenty-four internal constituents (*dhātu*) of the heroes who are established in the external maṇḍala wheel. By this, the summary of the fourth chapter is stated. Regarding "those established on the path of yoga": the nominative plural is used in the sense of the instrumental plural.

Yoga consists of the meditation on the mandala circle through the sequence beginning with the instantaneous form (*jhaṭityākāra*) and so forth; its path is the way, characterized as the location that serves as the basis for that meditation. This means [the practice] by those established therein and devoted thereto. By this, the summary of the fifth chapter is provided.

Regarding the word "concealed" (*gopitam*): The Blessed One taught the twelve primary weapons of the twelve-armed Śrī Heruka in the second chapter of the subtle *Mūlatantra*, because the weapons of the two-armed Blessed One alone are explained there, while they are not mentioned for the others. For this very reason, he says: "In that manner" (*tathā*), meaning by that method explicitly stated by his own throat; "in the Tantra" (*tantre*), meaning in the *Mūlatantra* which is of a summary nature. By this, the summary of the sixth chapter is stated.

It follows the sequence (*anuloma*). This is because, immediately after the meditation on the mandala consisting of the five wheels, one abandons the sequential order by concealing other meditations and drawing in the Knowledge Wheel (*jñānacakra*) through the two armor-mantras, thereby explaining the meditation according to the manifest order. By this, the summary of the seventh and eighth chapters is revealed.

Regarding the term *uddeśam*: it is because activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) have been taught according to their respective possibilities by way of indicating the three bodies (*kāya*). For this very reason, he says "as follows" (*yathā*): because the two bodies [the Enjoyment Body and the Emanation Body] are indicated according to the sequence of activity, and the Dharma Body is indicated according to the sequence of cessation. By this, there is a summary of the ninth chapter, which is characterized by non-differentiation (*abheda*).

"Instruction" (*nirdeśa*) refers to the detailed explanation, beginning from the first chapter, of the characteristics of conduct (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*) subsumed under non-concentrated yoga (*asamāhita-yoga*) and the characteristics of the tenth offering (*pūjā-lakṣaṇa*), once concentrated yoga (*samāhita-yoga*) has been established; by this, the summary of the tenth chapter is indicated.

"Detailed instruction" (*pratinirdeśa*) refers to the detailed explanation of universal purity (*sarva-viśuddhi*) once both concentrated yoga and its opposite have been completed; by this, the summary of the eleventh chapter is indicated.
"Entirely" (*samastam*) means "without remainder," because the two sequences are explained by means of the exposition of the ultimate reality. By this, the summary of the twelfth chapter is stated.

"The rule of convention" (*saṃketavidhim*) refers to the assignment of names to external sites such as the *pīṭhas* by way of their internal locations, and to the investigation of the terminology regarding the union of the four heroes and hand-worship. By this, the summary of the pair of chapters—the thirteenth and fourteenth—is stated.

"Supreme" (*uttama*) means that it is preeminent because, by the instruction "the vow of conduct" (*caryāvratam*), the purification of the six [factors] beginning with the *mudrā* through the gateway of mantra is explained. By this, the summary of the fifteenth chapter is stated. "By which" (*yena*) means simply by knowing the procedure for the movement and by practicing it. "The practitioner" (*sādhaka*) refers to one who accomplishes the two sequences taught in the *Saṃcāra-tantra*. "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) means he shall attain the accomplishment characterized by the certainty of the *mahāmudrā* and the transformation into Śrī Heruka. By this, the summary of the sixteenth chapter is stated. "By the yoga of thirty-seven" (*saptatriṃśad-yogena*).
By means of a ritual application (*prayoga*) of that same number, characterized by the manifestation of the *ḍākinīs* and so forth as the goddesses Māmakī and the rest;

"factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*) refers to the factors (*pakṣa*) or limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), which is the nature of Śrī Heruka in the form of unobscured gnosis (*jñāna*). These exist in the form of the display of the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) for the sake of the sign of the true meaning.
"Established" (*vyavasthita*) means they abide in that very form, exactly as they have been described in the Yoga, Kriyā, and other Tantras.

"World" (*loka*) refers to that which is comprised within the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). "Even a single [thing] having been manifested" means having cultivated it to the ultimate limit of excellence through cultivation. "Renowned" means that phenomena appear in a form made vivid by the consciousness of the yogi. "The supreme world of Śrī Heruka" means that although [the world] is in reality non-existent, it is displayed in the form of the maṇḍala and its deities for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. By this, the summary of the seventeenth chapter is stated.
An exposition on the essential body of the meaning of the entire Tantra. || 4 ||

Having thus established the promise of the exposition, the Blessed One, indicating how he will demonstrate the purification of the deities within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, says: "First of all," and so forth.
Having superimposed a specific location in the form of mountain caves and the like...

A yogi who has been consecrated and authorized according to the procedures taught in the tantras, and who has applied himself to the study of various tantras, should first of all—having thoroughly purified that place with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and other substances, and having duly rendered it free from obstacles through offerings (*bali*) and so forth—at the time of sleep, form the conviction (*adhimukti*) that "I am resting within the *dharmadhātu*.

Subsequently, at the time of dawn, upon hearing the clamor of birds and the like, he should conceive the conviction that the four goddesses have exhorted him there, and rely upon the awakening of the *dharmadhātu*.

Having emerged [from meditative absorption] and performed the purification of the sense-fields, and having carried out the cleansing of the mouth and so forth with scented water mixed with pills of the five nectars and other substances, one should—
assuming the pride of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and resolving, "I shall act for the benefit of sentient beings"—
sit upon a soft cushion and perform the examination of one's own mind and the protection of oneself according to the instructions.
One should begin with the bases such as the aggregates (*skandhas*) for the sake of turning back the ordinary ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

He says that very thing: "by the Lord of Yoga" (*yogeśvareṇa*). Yoga consists of the cultivation of the two stages; "Lord" (*īśvara*) therein means one who is independent, that is, autonomous. Alternatively, those whose state is external to this [system] are non-yogins; in comparison to them, those who cultivate the Tantras of Action (*kriyā*) and so forth are yogins. Because he is liberated through the Yoginī-tantras and others, being more distinguished than those [other] yogins, he is the "Lord of Yoga," by whom [the teaching was given].

Having meditated upon the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) according to the method taught in the *Abhisamaya* and following the system of the Pāramitā Tantras, one should generate the divine pride (*abhimāna*)—the identification with the deities within the five aggregates, such as form and so forth—in order to eliminate ordinary ego-clinging. "Should be generated" means it should be accomplished with a firm mind. (5)

Having thus established the general outline regarding the purification of the deities within the aggregates and so forth, he speaks first of the empowerment of the aggregates and so forth in order to provide their detailed explanation, beginning with "the aggregate of form," and so on.

In this regard, the instruction is as follows: at the head, navel, throat, secret place, heart, and the region above that, one should meditate upon the six Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) born from the transformations of *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jīṃ*, *khaṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *hrīṃ*. They are the Body, Knowledge, Speech, and Action Vajras, who are Śrī Heruka and Saṃvara. They have one face and two arms, their colors conforming to their respective families, and they sit in the vajra-posture upon lion, horse, peacock, garuḍa, elephant, and preta thrones, which rest upon double-lotuses, moons, and suns transformed from the syllable *pa*. Adorned with the five mudrās, holding the wheel, bell, and so forth, they consist of the three beings and are in union with their respective goddesses; thus say the feet of our supreme guru.

Alternatively, on the plane of syllables (*akṣarabhūmi*), for the sake of sentient beings, one should perform the empowerment of the aggregates (*skandhādhiṣṭhāna*) according to the sequence of mantras by means of visualization (*adhimukti*) as follows: upon the aforementioned six syllables of one’s own family color, located on the right side of a universal lotus and wheel in these very same places, as before.
This is precisely what is said: "The aggregate of form" refers to the head;

"Vairocana" refers to [the deity] specifically by virtue of his white color and his nature as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), because he illuminates—that is, makes manifest. "The aggregate of sensation" refers to the navel.

Because pleasure, pain, and so forth consist of the nature of feeling (*vedanā*), [the deity] is that [feeling]. "Vajrasūrya" means that, like a sun, he is a sun by virtue of being identical with the vajra—that is, the sun characterized by the wisdom of equality—and because he appears like the sun due to having that as his essence, he is Ratnasaṃbhava; or alternatively, because he is the form of the purification of the red element (*raktadhātu*). Regarding the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*): it is at the throat. Because one forms perceptions such as "bitter" after having experienced the six tastes and so forth, [the deity] is Padmanarteśvara.

Like a lotus, being unstained by the defect of mud, he remains untainted by passion and the like; thus, because he is the sovereign lord (*īśvara*) over the subsequent characteristic of investigating the welfare of sentient beings, Amitābha is characterized by the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Because he is the nature of the purification of the element of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he is the sovereign lord, independent (*svatantra*), in the dance characterized by falling upon the excellent limb of the Lotus Goddess (*padmadevī*).
He is the "aggregate of formations" (*saṃskāraskandha*) in the secret place, because at the time of the second consecration, he brings about the specific formations of the disciple.

Regarding "Vajrarāja": because he reigns—that is, illuminates—by means of the indivisible characteristic of the activities of sentient beings like a vajra, Amoghasiddhi is the embodiment of the knowledge of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
He is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) located in the heart.
He is called Vajrasattva because of his thorough knowledge of the sense objects.

Regarding *vajra*, because he possesses the intention (*abhiprāya*) for the nature of the *sattva* which is the form of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu-jñāna*, and because he is the embodiment of the fruit of Vajrasattva, he is Akṣobhya.

"The state of all Tathāgatas" means that he is the locus of the seed-syllables of all Tathāgatas upon the heart. "Śrī Herukavajra" refers to the sixth Tathāgata, whose essence consists of the four doors of liberation (*catur-vimokṣamukha*). (6)

Having thus explained the basis of the aggregates (*skandha-adhiṣṭhāna*), he speaks of the basis of the sense-bases (*āyatana-adhiṣṭhāna*): "In the two eyes, Mohavajra. As before, upon the *viśvapadma*, moon, and sun mandalas over the two eyes, there is Mohavajra, transformed from the syllable *Oṃ*. He is so called because, having abandoned his own object, he is deluded regarding other objects. He is Mohavajra because he is both delusion (*moha*) and a vajra, being empty of substantial reality (*vastu-śūnyatva*). He is the Great Powerful One (*Mahābala*) of the Body Wheel and so forth; he has one face, two arms, and holds a wheel and its bell; he is white. "In the two ears, Dveṣavajra."
In the two ears, as before, upon the seats, there is Dveṣavajra, transformed from the syllable *Haṃ*, as described previously.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is the aversion toward other objects through the abandonment of one's own object; and this is both hatred and a vajra, as before.
He is the first of the Citta-cakra, with one face, two arms, and a severed skull (*khaṇḍakapāla*), black in color, and holding a vajra and its bell.

Regarding "of the two nostrils": in the two nostril-pits, by means of the transformation of form as before, there is *īrṣyāvajra*. Because he avoids his own sound (*nijarāva*) and is a vajra whose nature is jealousy arising from other objects, and because he is as before, he is called *īrṣyāvajra*.
Virūpākṣa, who is at the beginning of the speech-chakra, has one face and two arms; as before, he is red in color and holds a lotus and its bell.

"Vaktra" refers to the cavity of the mouth; as before, he is born from the syllable Ā. "Rāgavajra" refers to the sprout of the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*): he has one face and two arms, and holds a lotus and its bell. Because of passion (*rāga*), he focuses exclusively on his own object of focus by abandoning all other objects immediately after they appear. And because he is both that [being] and a *vajra*, as previously stated, he is called Rāgavajra.

"Touch" (*sparśa*) refers to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), its predominant form, or its indicative sign (*liṅga*). As before, he is born from the syllable *Oṃ* as Mātsaryavajra. Because of envy (*mātsarya*) toward other objects after having abandoned one's own tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*), he is both that [envy] and a vajra; because of emptiness, he is Mātsaryavajra. At the end of the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*), Vajrasattva has one face, two arms, holds his own emblem, and is white.
"In all sense-bases" (*sarvāyataneṣu*) means in the mind, at the location of the heart.

Just as before, when the syllable *hūṃ* has emerged, there is "Aiśvaryavajra. In every object, or in the *dharmadhātu*, which consists of seven substances, he is both the Lord (*īśvara*) because of his sovereignty and lack of dependence, and the Vajra; thus, as before, Aiśvaryavajra is within the mind-circle (*cittacakra*), in the Vajra-body, two-armed, one-faced, holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, and black in color.

This is what is meant: just as in the procedure of the Great Yoga (mahāyoga), Kṣitigarbha and the others are meditated upon in the six sense-bases (āyatana) through the transformation of the seed-syllables *kṣiṃ*, *jaṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *ṣkaṃ*, and *saṃ*—appearing in forms such as three-faced and six-armed—so too here, one should perform the consecration of the sense-bases by including the heroes from beginning to end within the three wheels; such is the tradition (*āmnāya*). || 7 ||

Having thus explained the basis of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), he speaks, indicating the intent to explain the basis of the elements (*dhātu*): "Of Śrī Heruka. This refers to the yogin who possesses that form. "Purification of the elements" means the complete cleansing of the five elements characterized as the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). The word "thus" means by the method that will be explained. He states that very point: "The earth element," and so forth.

Herein is the instruction: In the four wheels beginning with the *nirmāṇa*, via the central channel—or rather, through the gateways of the body-channels which have the nature of hardness, moisture, heat, motion, and space, and which function as the movement and non-movement of unstable blood and so forth, and as warmth—in the locations of the head, one should visualize the seed-syllables *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*, and *khaṃ*. These correspond to the Ḍākinīs Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, Rūpiṇī, and Vārāhī; they are single-faced and four-armed, possessing black, yellow, reddish-brown, dark green, and red complexions respectively for their primary faces and limbs, and they hold a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and a flaying-knife (*kartī*).

Specifically, the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī should be placed; she has three faces and six arms, her central face and body are reddish, while the right and left faces are blue and white respectively. She holds a flaying knife, a skull-cup, a noose, a goad, a raised index finger, and a severed head. This is precisely what is stated: "the earth element. The meaning of this is already explained. She is called *Pātanī* because she is the Ḍākinī who [subdues] the conceptualization of the earth element.
She is called *Māriṇī* because she is the Lāmā who slays the conceptualization of the water element.

*Ākarṣaṇī* (The Attractor) is so called because she makes the conceptualization of the fire element (*tejodhātu*) free from appearance (*nirābhāsīkaraṇa*) by attracting it. *Narteśvarī* (The Mistress of Dance) is so called because she is the mistress or sovereign over the dancing that occurs through the power of joy after having warded off the conceptualization of the wind element (*vāyudhātu*), characterized by the movement of all limbs.

*Padmajvālinī* (She Who Blazes with Lotuses) is so called because, like a lotus, she is unstained by defects, and because she extracts the conceptualization of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) like a net. (8)

Having thus explained the empowerment of the elements (*dhātu*), he says "In this way," and so forth, in order to state the conclusion regarding the empowerment of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so on.

"By the method" means by the principle just explained. "In the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields" refers to the locations previously mentioned. "The divine ego-sense" is intended as the antidote to the ordinary ego-sense. "Should be generated" means it should be accomplished and made firm.
Thus ends the detailed commentary on the first chapter of the *Upadeśānusāriṇī*, a commentary on the *Yoginīsaṃcāratantra* composed by the venerable Paṇḍita Ācārya Alakakalaśa. 1.

Thus, having established the exposition of the purification of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields as the antidote to ordinary ego-grasping by means of the first chapter, he states the second chapter—characterized by the exposition of the factors conducive to enlightenment—in order to explain the cultivation of the mundane and supramundane paths, beginning with the words "atha" and so forth. This follows immediately after the exposition on the cultivation of the purification of the aggregates and so on.
"Thirty-seven" refers to that specific number.
"Factors conducive to enlightenment" (bodhipākṣikā dharmāḥ) [is the term used].

Unobstructed gnosis, which is subsumed within the stage of a Buddha, is enlightenment (*bodhi*); the "wings" (*pakṣa*) are those things existing on that side, because they are causes conducive to its attainment.

They are indeed "the dharmas," because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) characterized by wisdom, vigor, meditative concentration, and so forth. "By means of the yoga of the deity" means by means of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or application (*prayoga*) whose nature consists of the thirty-seven yoginīs, such as the *ḍākinīs* and others.
"They are to be joined" (*yuñjanīyā*) means they are to be joined in the form of their purification; that is to say, they are to be cultivated by a yogin who has faith in the Mantra Mahāyāna.

Having thus established the summary (uddeśa), he speaks in order to provide the detailed explanation (nirdeśa), saying: "Those too... This refers to those factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika) which are applied in the yoga of the deity. To the question "Which ones?"—meaning "Of what form and of what nature are they?"—this is an inquiry concerning their number. || 1 ||
He states the answer: "The application of mindfulness to the body.

It should be understood that each of these applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth is determined by four points: namely, the purpose of their cultivation, their essential nature, their classification according to the path and the individual, and their excellence as distinguished from that of the Śrāvakas and others. Among these, first, the purpose of cultivating the applications of mindfulness is the entry into the four truths, as stated by the Blessed One to Maitreya:

"Because of corruption, because of being the cause of thirst, because of being a substantial entity, and because of non-delusion, there is the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness for the sake of entering the Four Truths.
This is its meaning: for it is by means of the body that corruption is manifested, insofar as it has the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
For in that way, they perceive every object associated with the outflows as noble suffering; thus, feeling is the cause of craving.
Because of the statement that "craving has feeling as its condition," one enters into the truth of origination through the investigation of that [feeling].
The mind is the basis for the attachment to a self.
Because the self is subverted by valid cognition and lacks any means of proof, it is precisely that [self] which serves as the basis for such dogmatic adherence.

By examining that [self], one enters into the truth of cessation, since fear regarding the annihilation of the self disappears. By examining phenomena (*dharma*), one enters into the truth of the path, due to the disappearance of delusion concerning defiled and purified phenomena.
Therefore, at the outset, the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is established for the purpose of entering into the four truths.
As for their essential nature: those things through which mindfulness is established in contemplation are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
There are four, distinguished by their objects. Regarding this, it is said in the Sūtra:

"One dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, in the external body, and in the internal-external body. One does not direct discursive thoughts associated with the body. And that is through the yoga of non-apprehension; ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, one abides."

In this context, "the internal body" refers to one's own sixfold [sense] bases beginning with the eye; "the external body" refers to conditioned things outside of one's own body; "the internal-external body" refers to the remaining material elements belonging to one's own body; and "contemplating the body" means contemplating the true nature (dharmatā) of the body.

"Accompanied by the body" means accompanied by the perceptions (*saṃjñā*) of the body and so forth. "Discursive thoughts" (*vitarka*) refers to conceptualizations (*vikalpa*); he reflects upon them such as: "This body is permanent or impermanent," "pleasure or suffering," and so on. "Ardent" (*ātāpī*) is due to his application (*prayoga*) with constancy and respect. "Clearly comprehending" (*saṃprajānan*) is due to his connection with clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) through observation. "Mindful" (*smṛtimān*) is due to his connection with mindfulness (*smṛti*) whose nature is non-forgetfulness and which brings about non-distraction.

He states the benefit of these very qualities—prowess, wisdom, and mindfulness—in the verse beginning with "having subdued": *loke* means among worldly phenomena such as gain, fame, pleasure, and praise; *abhidhyā* is greed, and *daurmanasya* is the suffering of loss and lack of fame; *nityam* means constantly; having subdued—that is, having abandoned—these greed and dejection.

In this way, it should be applied to the external body and so forth. Likewise, regarding feeling (*vedanā*), one dwells contemplating feelings—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—inwardly, outwardly, and both inwardly and outwardly, as previously described. Furthermore, with respect to the momentariness of the mind, which is devoid of prior and posterior limits, one dwells contemplating feelings associated with internal and external phenomena that are of a wholesome, unwholesome, or dual nature. He does not engage in discursive thoughts accompanied by those feelings. The phrase "ardent" (*ātāpī*) and so forth should be applied accordingly. It is the same for mental objects (*dharma*).

The classification [of the foundations of mindfulness] is made by way of the distinction between the path and the individuals; furthermore, it pertains specifically to the mundane level. On the path, during the stage of the accumulation of merit (*saṃbhārabhūmi*), which is another synonym for the "examination of things," this belongs only to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Primarily for one abiding in the desire realm or the form realm, the foundations of mindfulness consist of the examination of the characteristics of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, both in their specific and general characteristics. Their excellence, distinguished from that of the Śrāvakas and others, should be understood through both summary and detailed exposition.
In that regard, first, the summary is presented in three aspects, as stated by the Blessed One himself:
"Distinction [of the bodhisattva's path] arises from the object, mental attention, and attainment.

This is its meaning: for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the objects are shadows and so forth belonging to their own continuum; for Bodhisattvas, however, they belong to both their own and others' continua.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attend to shadows and so forth through aspects such as impermanence; bodhisattvas, however, do so by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Furthermore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so on solely for the sake of dissociation from the body and other aggregates. For bodhisattvas, however, it is neither for the sake of association nor for dissociation, but rather for the attainment of non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).

Having thus explained the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), in order to dispel the delusion of those who take pride in being reciters or possessors of books, the cultivation of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) should be established hereafter in its proper sequence.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness by Bodhisattvas is distinguished from that of the Śrāvakas and others by fourteen aspects,
as it has been said:
It is distinguished by its basis, its counteragent, and likewise by its entry,
as well as by its object, mental attention, and attainment.
"Through conformity and following, through thorough knowledge and arising, through measure and through supremacy, cultivation [is perfected] by way of full attainment. (MAvSū 18.43–44).
In that regard, first, "by way of basis" means relying upon the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and meditation within the Mahāyāna.

In terms of being an antidote (*pratipakṣataḥ*), because it serves as the antidote to some of the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*)—namely, the notions of suffering, impermanence, and non-self—by means of entering into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) regarding the body and so forth.

In terms of entry (*avatārataḥ*), it is for the sake of entering into the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path by means of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) respectively; or alternatively, because one enters them oneself and causes others to enter them.
Immediately following this, the purpose (*prayojana*) has been explained.
In terms of the object (*ālambana*), it is because it takes the bodies and so forth of all sentient beings as its object.

How [is it practiced] in terms of mental attention (*manaskāra*)? It is by relying on five kinds of causes, through the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of the body and so forth. In terms of attainment (*prāpti*), it is neither for the sake of conjunction with nor for the sake of disjunction from the body and so forth. In terms of conformity (*ānūkūlya*), it is by way of conforming to the perfections (*pāramitā*), because they serve as the antidotes to their opposites.

In terms of following along (*anuvṛtti*), it is by following along with worldly people, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, because one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that are brought about by them, for the purpose of instructing them.

The body is fully understood through the thorough knowledge of its being like an illusion, because it appears as a form that is likewise unreal; sensation is fully understood through the thorough knowledge of its being like a dream, because it is likewise a false experience; the mind is fully understood as naturally luminous, like space; and phenomena are fully understood as adventitious, like the adventitious dust, smoke, clouds, and mist that afflict the sky. Furthermore, regarding birth: when one intentionally takes birth in existence as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) or similar being, possessing the excellence of a distinguished body, sensations, and so forth, there is no defilement therein.
[In terms of measure (*mātrā*): because the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is superior even to others who possess only a mild degree of it;

[in terms of excellence (*parama*): because for those who have reached perfection through having naturally sharp faculties, there is a cultivation that is effortless, integrated, and thoroughly blended; [in terms of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): because through the constant cultivation of that, it remains inexhaustible even in the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); [in terms of attainment (*samudāgama*): because it is fully realized throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and in Buddhahood. || 2 ||

In this way, in order to dispel the delusion of those who are conceited about their own books—thinking that the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are [the final stage]—and in order to present the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which follow in sequence even though the cultivation of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) has been set aside in the middle, he says: "The basis of psychic power consisting of desire" (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*).
Here too, as before, the determination should be understood through four points.

In this regard, first, the purpose of this cultivation is the attainment of stability for the mind—that is, the heating of its steadiness—for one who is established in the cultivation of vigor through the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*). As it has been said: "Therein, flexibility of stability exists for the fulfillment of all aims," and so forth.

Furthermore, as for their essential nature: *ṛddhi* refers to supramundane phenomena; because they serve as the basis (*pada-sthāna*) for that [stability], they are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
These, moreover, are fourfold, beginning with desire (*chanda*).
For instance, in someone who is intensely applied to that very [practice], there arises concentration characterized by one-pointedness of mind;

in someone else who is well-applied to the right exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*) for the abandoning of the unwholesome and the production of the wholesome; in someone else who purifies the mind by means of the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*);
and in yet another who correctly investigates: "By what subtle observation do my wholesome qualities manifest, or how should I thoroughly examine those qualities currently in operation?"

Thus, by correctly identifying the defects of concentration within the context of cultivation and performing their abandonment through the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are accomplished.
For instance, these defects of concentration are: laziness, loss of the object of focus, lethargy, as well as agitation, lack of effort, and excessive effort.
And for these, as appropriate, the eight formative forces of abandonment—consisting of zeal, energy, faith, pliancy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity—serve as the basis.

In that regard, the desire (chanda) consisting of the thought, "When indeed shall I produce mundane and supramundane meditative concentrations and attainments? is itself the basis for vigor (*vīrya*) which eradicates all unwholesome states; and that [vigor] is what is supported [by desire].
Faith (*śraddhā*) is the longing and conviction regarding the four higher qualities of realization (*adhigama-dharma*).

And that [faith] is the cause of the basis, which is zeal (*chanda*), because there is a longing when there is conviction through faith. And preceded by that [zeal], there is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), which is the serviceability of body and mind; this is the fruit of the supported, which is effort (*vyāyāma*). As it has been said: "The basis, then the supported, its cause, and its fruit.
Through these four, for the sake of abandoning the fault characterized by laziness, concentration of zeal (*chanda-samādhi*) is accomplished.
Concentration of vigor (*vīrya-samādhi*) arises from the abandonment, by means of mindfulness belonging to the side of calm (*śamatha*), of the loss of the object of focus.

The concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*) arises from the abandonment of lethargy and excitement through clear comprehension (*samprajanya*). Clear comprehension should be understood as the perception of dwellings and groves, consisting in the production of mental attention toward things to be experienced, according to their respective order.

The concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*) arises from the abandonment of non-exertion and exertion through volition (*cetanā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). In this context, volition is the formative activity of the mind, while equanimity is the state of being undefiled.

Regarding the summary and detailed classification according to the divisions of the paths and individuals: this occurs precisely on the mundane path—the stage of the preliminary desire for meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—during the subsequent phase of the stage of the great equipment (*adhimātra-sambhāra-bhūmi*), wherein these [qualities] are accomplished by the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) alone.

Furthermore, their distinction from that of the Śrāvakas and others is as previously stated; they should be understood as being distinguished solely by the fact that they concern one's own welfare. (3)
Having thus established the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), he speaks in order to explain the faculties (*indriya*), beginning with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

Here too, as before, the determination should be understood through four points. First, regarding the purpose of cultivation: it is the mastery over aspiration and so forth, achieved by bringing to completion the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) once the mind has been made pliant through the bases of psychic power. As it is said: "Once the roots conducive to liberation have been planted, [mastery arises] through the predominance of aspiration and application."
"For it is the non-forgetfulness of the object, as well as the non-diffusion and investigation [of it].

Furthermore, as for its essential nature: it is called a faculty (*indriya*) because of its ruling (*indana*). This is based on the root list (*dhātupāṭha*), which states that the root *idi* means "supreme sovereignty.
The five beginning with faith become faculties because they attain sovereignty over the production of supramundane qualities.

Here too, there is a twofold explanation: because for one who is well-practiced in the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), certainty arises upon seeing signs when higher distinctions emerge; thus, conviction regarding the realization of the Teacher and his disciples is born. Therefore, this faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)—due to the preeminence of faith—it should be understood that there is a corresponding preeminence of energy (*vīrya*) and the other faculties.

Alternatively, for one whose mind has become pliant through the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), there are the five faculties (*indriya*): faith, by virtue of the predominance of the desire for the power of the wholesome factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) that have been planted; vigor, by virtue of the predominance of application; mindfulness, by virtue of the predominance of not forgetting the object of focus; concentration, by virtue of the predominance of absence of regret; and wisdom, by virtue of the predominance of discernment.

Regarding the summary and detailed classification according to the divisions of the paths and individuals: on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), which is another synonym for the preparatory path of clear realization (*abhisamayaprāyogikamārga*), during the stages of "Heat" (*ūṣma*) and "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), their accomplishment belongs specifically to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) as distinguished from the Śrāvakas and others. Their excellence, however, should be understood through the same three points as before, by way of the distinction in their own welfare (*svārtha*). || 4 ||

Having thus explained the faculties (*indriya*), he speaks in order to explain the powers (*bala*): "the power of faith" (*śraddhābala*). Here too, as before, the establishment [of the meaning] should be understood through four points.

In that regard, first, the purpose of cultivation is the production of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereby the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth—namely, patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*)—come to be for the sake of perfecting the roots of virtue conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

Furthermore, their essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of faith and the other [faculties], which have already been explained for the former [stage]. Their status as "powers" (*bala*), however, is due to their being uncrushable by opposing factors such as Māra, and because they cannot be assailed by the so-called impurities of laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and faulty wisdom—this being distinguished according to the paths and individuals. Their classification in summary is again as before. These very faculties, belonging to the mental continuum of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), are the [five] powers. Abhisamaya occurs precisely on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) during the embryonic state of the stages of Receptivity (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), because of the further increase [of these faculties] during the remaining path, which is another synonym for the path of cultivation.

The classification of the equal [perfection] by way of its distinction from that of the Śrāvakas and others should be understood through exactly three points, as before, because it serves as an antidote solely for one's own welfare. (5)

Having thus explained the powers (*balas*), he speaks in order to describe the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅgas*), saying: "the factor of enlightenment that is concentration" (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Here too, the systematic presentation should be understood by means of four points.

Among these, first, the purpose of cultivation is for the sake of generating the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) in one who has already attained the four stages beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Furthermore, its essential nature is that awakening (*bodhi*) or perfect awakening (*saṃbodhi*) which arises from the realization of things as they truly are on the path of vision. It has seven limbs, and these consist of the forms of calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and both together. Among them, the pliancies (*praśrabdhi*) dependent upon concentration (*samādhi*) belong to the side of calm abiding; the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), joy (*prīti*), and vigor (*vīrya*) belong to the side of insight; while mindfulness (*smṛti*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) [belong to both]. Therein, concentration is explained as follows: when one whose mind is deluded becomes connected with the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering and so forth through the equality of all phenomena, this is called the limb of awakening of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Likewise, through the attainment of meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as the Gaganagañja, there is the fulfillment of intended aims; and from that, meditative absorption arises. This is the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). That which is the exertion, the application, and the strength toward the factors of enlightenment even for a single moment is called the factor of enlightenment of vigor. Alternatively, it is the engagement of vigor for the sake of attaining swift superknowledge (*abhijñā*), just as a king [exerts himself] to travel across the great earth bounded by the oceans in search of his own precious jewels and treatises.
As it is said: "And his vigor proceeds swiftly toward complete awakening."

Regarding the factor of enlightenment that is joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*): through the joy of the Dharma, the mind becomes free from dejection and one dispels the afflictions (*kleśa*). By virtue of having initiated vigor, his worldly qualities increase. Consequently, that joy constantly gladdens both the entire body and the mind, just as a precious jewel (*maṇiratna*) gladdens a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) by means of its extraordinary radiance.
As it has been said:
"And by the increase of the light of the Dharma, one is surely filled with joy.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment that is pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Because of the eradication of all functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) to be abandoned by vision, there is the accomplishment of a distinguished happiness, just as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) experiences bliss through the jewel of a woman. As it has been said:
"Through liberation from all obscurations, one attains bliss by means of pliancy.

This refers to the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). It is the knowledge that investigates the eighty-four thousand aggregates of teachings (*dharmaskandha*) through their distinctions, such as the provisional and the definitive, or the conventional and the ultimate, for the purpose of shattering all signs of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), just as the precious elephant [is used] for the destruction of empty conceptualization.
As it was said:
"And his investigation is for the sake of destroying all signs of conceptual construction.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment called mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). It is that mindfulness by which one examines all phenomena, conquering what has not been conquered and abandoning what is to be abandoned, just as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) serves to conquer unconquered territories.
As it was said:
"Mindfulness operates everywhere for the sake of conquering the unconquered objects of knowledge.

Regarding the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): when those dharmas associated with mental joy or dejection are consumed by his mind and overwhelmed by worldly conditions, that constitutes his factor of enlightenment which is equanimity.

Alternatively, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is said to be non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). Thus, the Bodhisattva dwells everywhere according to his wish by means of the subsequent knowledge that takes that [non-conceptual state] as its object, because he approaches some things and departs from others. He establishes his residence through dwelling in non-conceptuality and through being free from effort (*nirvyāpāratā*). Just as the counselor-treasure (*pariṇāyaka-ratna*) of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) brings forward the fourfold army that is to be approached and removes that which is to be removed, and having gone there, establishes a residence wherever the fourfold army proceeds without fatigue.
As it has been said:
"Through equanimity, he dwells everywhere according to his wish;
through the non-conceptual state attained subsequently, the Supreme One always abides.
Thus, their essential nature is also described by way of the inclusion of the factors: therein, awakening is the basis, and mindfulness is [the support].
The intrinsic nature [of the factors of enlightenment] is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); the limb of departure is vigor (*vīrya*); the limb of benefit is joy (*prīti*).
The limb free from affliction is threefold, due to the distinction between the basis, the intrinsic nature, and the differentiation, in relation to *nirvāṇa*.

Among these, serenity (*prasrabdhi*) is the antidote to the dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) that are the cause of affliction; therefore, concentration (*samādhi*) is the basis for the absence of affliction; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is its intrinsic nature.
As it has been said:
"The limb of the basis, the limb of essential nature, and the third, the limb of departure;
the fourth is the limb of benefit, and the limb free from affliction is considered to be threefold."
"It has been taught here by way of its cause, its basis, and its intrinsic nature.

Thus, with respect to the distinctions of the path and the individuals, the collective classification is as follows: the supramundane clear realizations of the truths are established for noble individuals—predominantly as the antidotes to the afflictions belonging to the three realms—according to their respective capacities.

Furthermore, their excellence, distinguished from that of the śrāvakas and others, consists in being characterized by a penetration of the four truths that is distinct [from theirs] and by the accumulation of perfections which serves as the antidote to those [afflictions]. — [This occurs] through the penetration of the all-pervading dharmadhātu. (6)

Having thus explained the factors of enlightenment (*saṃbodhyaṅga*), he speaks in order to describe the noble eightfold path, beginning with "right view" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Here too, a fourfold arrangement should be observed. First, regarding the purpose of its cultivation: for one who has fully understood and seen the truths, cultivation results in the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). As for its essential nature (*svarūpa*): right view is the vision that follows the realization of things as they truly are, occurring after the stage of the factors of enlightenment and consisting in the discernment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). [Next is] "right intention" (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).

The establishment of that very realization is right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*); and since the Blessed One has established that in the Sūtras and other teachings, it is precisely through them that there is entry, because one realizes its meaning by means of them.
