Regarding "right speech" (*samyagvāk*): right speech, along with the triad of right action, right livelihood, and right effort, constitutes the purification of the three types of activity, because they comprise the activities of both speech and body.

The cultivation of the counteragents consists of right effort, mindfulness, and concentration, which respectively counteract the obscuration of the knowable, the obscuration of the path, and the obscuration to the special qualities. For it is thus: by means of right effort, one who is untiring over a long period of time cultivates the counteragent to the obscuration of the knowable. By means of right mindfulness, because there is no sinking or agitation regarding the signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity, one cultivates the counteragent to the obscuration that prevents the manifestation of the path.

Through right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), one cultivates the antidote to the obscuration for the sake of bringing forth the distinguished qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*). [This is accomplished] by means of the aggregates (*skandha*). Among these, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), and right speech (*samyagvāk*)—namely, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*). Therein, the discernment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) consists of right view, right intention, and right speech; and this [aggregate] possesses both components according to the principle that will be explained hereafter.

Or, by means of its correct origination and the attainment thereof, the limb of inspiring confidence in others is threefold: right speech, right action, and right livelihood. For through these, in their respective order, confidence arises in three respects: through right action, in terms of ethical discipline (*śīla*), because one refrains from what ought not to be done; through right livelihood, in terms of austerity (*saṃlekha*), because one seeks robes and other requisites in accordance with the Dharma and in moderation, according to the principle that "one should discard anything beyond the three robes. The limb of the antidote to opposing factors is threefold, distinguished as right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

For these are, respectively, the antidotes to the affliction (*kleśa*), the mastery over the secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) to be abandoned—namely, lethargy and excitement—and the production of the distinguished qualities that are the opposites [of those obstacles]. As it has been said: "Determination, then attainment, and the threefold confidence of others; The adverse side, the antidote, and the factors of the path—thus it is eightfold."
"In view and in ethical conduct, as well as in austerity, there is the desire for instruction from others;
[these constitute] the state of being an antidote to the afflictions, the secondary afflictions, and the lack of mastery. Thus it is said.

When summarized according to the distinctions of the path and the person, the detailed classification occurs on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is another term for the path of purification and deliverance. This belongs only to the trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the truths, and not to anyone else. Furthermore, its distinction from the Śrāvakas and others should be understood as arising from the cultivation of the antidote to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). (7)

Having thus explained the Noble Eightfold Path, he speaks for the purpose of explaining the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), beginning with the words: "of wholesome states that have not yet arisen," and so forth.

Here too, the determination of the meaning should be understood through the four points as before. In this context, there is first the cultivation of exertion, the thorough knowledge of the adversaries to the foundations of mindfulness, the means for their abandonment, and the arousal of vigor. As it has been said:
"When the adversary and the antidote are thoroughly known in every respect..."
"For indeed, energy proceeds in four ways for the sake of abandoning those [faults].
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, as for its essential nature:
